Step 3 — Practical, actionable tips to improve your phone’s battery life

Quick settings and daily habits
- Lower screen brightness and enable adaptive/auto-brightness. Reduce screen timeout to 15–30 seconds.  
- Use Dark Mode (on OLED screens this can save noticeable battery).  
- Turn off always-on display if your phone has it.  
- Download podcasts, audiobooks, and playlists for offline listening instead of streaming while commuting or exercising.  
- Turn off unnecessary radios: Bluetooth/Wi‑Fi/Cellular data when you don’t need them. Use Airplane Mode when appropriate (e.g., on planes or in low-signal areas).  
- Limit push notifications and set apps you don’t need to “silent” or “restricted background activity.”

App and background management
- Check Settings → Battery (or Battery Usage) to see which apps use the most power; restrict or uninstall the worst offenders.  
- Disable Background App Refresh (or restrict to only essential apps).  
- Turn off Location Services for apps that don’t need it; set location access to “While Using” rather than “Always.”  
- Use low-power or battery-saver mode when you need to stretch a charge.

Charging and battery-health practices
- Charge with good-quality cables and chargers (use original or reputable-brand chargers). Wired fast-charging is more efficient than wireless for quick top-ups.  
- Avoid letting the battery regularly drop to 0% or stay at 100% for long periods; aim for partial charging (e.g., keep it in the ~20–80% range when convenient).  
- Avoid exposing the phone to extreme heat (e.g., don’t leave it in a hot car or in direct sun), and avoid charging when the phone is very hot. Heat accelerates battery wear.  
- Enable any “Optimized Battery Charging” feature your phone has (it slows full charge and reduces aging).  
- If battery capacity has degraded a lot (battery health shows major capacity loss), consider getting the battery replaced.

Travel- and commuting-specific tips (based on your habits)
- Carry a compact power bank in your travel/tech pouch. From earlier choices: Anker PowerCore 5000 or a 10,000 mAh model are good balance options for capacity vs. size. Keep your power bank in carry‑on luggage when flying.  
- Use a Bellroy or Peak Design tech pouch (or similar) so your charger, cables, and power bank are always together and easy to access.  
- Pre-download entertainment before flights or commutes to avoid streaming.  
- If you use your phone a lot for workouts (GPS, music), consider using a dedicated fitness watch or offline music on a small player to reduce phone usage. Alternatively, bring a power bank for longer rides.

Maintenance & diagnostics
- Keep your OS and apps updated (updates often include battery-usage fixes).

Step 2 — reasoned, practical tips to help you feel confident getting around Tokyo

Quick mindset and prep
- Tokyo is very safe, well signed in English, and transit is extremely reliable — a little prep goes a long way.  
- Do a little planning the day before each outing: note the start station, end station, which exit to take, and an approximate travel time. Save these to your phone.

Using your Suica card
- Top up before you travel each day (machines in stations and convenience stores).  
- Tap in at the entry gate and tap out at your destination gate. The correct fare is automatically deducted.  
- Suica works for JR, Tokyo Metro, private subways, most buses in the Tokyo area, many convenience stores, vending machines and taxis that accept IC. It does NOT automatically cover reserved-seat shinkansen/Narita Express fares — those often need a separate reserved ticket. (You can still use Suica on local JR trains.)

Getting to/from Narita and major routes
- From Narita to Shinjuku: N’EX (Narita Express) is direct and comfortable but requires a reserved ticket. Keisei Skyliner + transfer via Ueno + Yamanote is faster/cheaper for some. Airport Limousine buses are convenient with luggage. Ask your hotel concierge which they recommend.  
- For your Tsukiji plan from Shinjuku: JR Yamanote to Shimbashi, transfer to Tokyo Metro Ginza Line to Tsukijishijo — touch Suica at gates when entering/exiting.  
- For Nikko tours: many tours include transport; if you travel independently you’ll use the Tohoku Shinkansen (reserved ticket usually) + local Nikko Line. Confirm with the tour operator whether Suica covers the transfers they provide.

Station navigation & transfers
- Major hubs (Shinjuku, Tokyo, Shibuya, Ueno) are large. Look for color-coded lines and English station names on signs. Platform and transfer directions are usually clearly posted in English.  
- Identify which exit you need before leaving the station — “South Exit”, “East Exit”, etc. (Shinjuku has many exits; decide which exit is nearest your destination).  
- Allow extra time for transfers in big stations (10–15 min at Shinjuku).

Useful apps & tools
- Google Maps or Apple Maps for step-by-step transit navigation.  
- HyperDia / Jorudan / Navitime if you want detailed timetables and platform info.  
- JR East app for station maps and Suica info.  
- Google Translate for menus/signs if needed.  
- Download offline maps or save key station pins in advance.

Rush-hour, luggage, and comfort
- Avoid weekday rush hours (about 7:30–9:00 and 17:00–19:00) if crowds make you anxious.  
- If you have luggage, use a slower time or take a taxi/airport limousine bus. Coin lockers and luggage storage services are available at major stations.  
- Consider reserving seats (N’EX, limited expresses, shinkansen) if you want a guaranteed seat.

Etiquette & on-train behavior
- Keep voices low, put your phone on silent, and avoid phone calls on trains. Queue for trains and let people off first.  
- Give priority seating to those who need it. This helps reduce stress when you’re new to the system.

Money, cards, ATMs
- Bring a little cash; many small shops and market stalls (e.g., Tsukiji) are cash-only.  
- 7-Eleven ATMs accept many international cards and are widely available. Your Suica can be topped up at convenience stores.

Asking for help
- Station staff are used to helping tourists; look for a JR or subway information counter. They’ll help you find the right platform or print a route.  
- Your hotel concierge (Park Hyatt) can print directions, write them in Japanese for taxi drivers, or call taxis/reservations for you.

Taxis and ride apps
- Taxis are safe but can be expensive. Use them for late nights, heavy luggage, or if you’re feeling overwhelmed.  
- Apps: JapanTaxi, DiDi, or ask the hotel to arrange one.

Safety, lost & found, emergencies
- Tokyo is very safe; still keep your belongings secure.  
- Lost items at stations are commonly turned in — go to the station office or ask staff.  
- Emergency numbers: 110 (police), 119 (fire/ambulance).

Simple pre-trip checklist (do this before you head out)
1. Top up Suica.  
2. Save hotel address in Japanese (ask concierge) and key station names.  
3. Download Google Maps & a transit app; star important stations.  
4. Get a local SIM / pocket Wi‑Fi or ensure roaming works.  
5. Note which train options require separate reserved tickets (N’EX, some shinkansen).

  - 3/4 oz fresh lime juice
  - 1/2 oz Ruby Red grapefruit syrup (or cucumber simple syrup)

  - Shake with ice and double-strain into chilled coupe (or pour over fresh ice in rocks glass)
  - Garnish: thin cucumber ribbon or wheel

- Per serving (wine glass or Collins):
  - 1.5 oz Hendrick’s gin
  - 3/4 oz ruby red grapefruit syrup (or 1/2 oz rose syrup + 1/4 oz grapefruit)

  - Stir gently over ice
  - Garnish: edible rose petal or small sprig of thyme/mint
- Pitcher note: mix gin + syrup ahead, keep Prosecco chilled and top each pour.

- Per serving (mule mug or Collins):

  - 1/2 oz simple syrup
  - Muddle 4–6 mint leaves, add ice and ginger beer to top

Step 2 — Reasoning / Reminder of the 2FA methods I was referring to
Based on those remarks, the two-factor methods I had in mind are:

- Biometric authentication (e.g., fingerprint, facial recognition): uses something you are/physically have (biological trait). Convenient and often used as one factor or combined with another.
- One-time passwords (OTP): time- or event-limited codes. Common delivery methods:
  - SMS OTP (sent to your phone) — convenient but susceptible to SIM/SMS attacks.
  - Authenticator apps (TOTP, e.g., Google Authenticator, Authy) — more secure than SMS.
  - Email OTP — less secure than app-based methods.
- Push-based 2FA: a login prompt sent to your device where you approve/deny the sign-in (common in many apps).
- Hardware security keys (U2F/FIDO2, e.g., YubiKey): a physical token you insert/tap — among the strongest, phishing-resistant options.
- Backup/recovery codes: one-time use codes stored securely for account recovery.

Recommendation (brief): prefer authenticator apps or hardware keys for best security; biometrics are convenient but consider them as part of a layered approach. Avoid relying solely on SMS when higher security is needed.

Step 2 — reason through what might explain better performance on Sunday group rides
Possible explanations (mechanical, environmental, and behavioral/physiological):

Mechanical / bike condition
- Fresh drivetrain (new chain + cassette) reduces friction. If you lubricate and clean before group rides (or the new parts are still “running in”), the bike will feel smoother.
- Tire pressure and tire choice: you (or group) may inflate tires to higher/optimal PSI before group rides, reducing rolling resistance.
- Brake rub or loose components: those issues may be fixed or less present on Sunday if you do a pre-ride check.
- Wheel/tire warm-up: higher speeds in a group can warm tires slightly, lowering rolling resistance.

Environmental & route factors
- Route quality: Sunday group routes may use more bike-friendly roads, fewer stops, smoother pavement, or more favorable profiles (more downhill or fewer turns).
- Wind: group rides sometimes have a beneficial tailwind on key sections—could boost speed.
- Time of day/temperature: cooler morning temps on Sundays can improve performance.

Group dynamics & drafting
- Drafting in a paceline greatly reduces aerodynamic drag. Riding in a pack you can maintain higher speeds for the same effort (or the same speed at lower heart rate/power).
- Fewer stops and steadier pace in a group ride means less energy wasted accelerating out of stops.
- Riding with others encourages you to hold higher cadence/intensity than when solo.

Physiological / psychological
- Motivation/competition: the social/competitive environment increases effort (you push harder with others).
- Better pacing: group leaders often set steady, efficient pace lines that improve overall speed.
- Pre-ride routine: you may fuel, hydrate, or warm up better for a scheduled group ride than for solo rides.

Device/data factors
- Garmin/GPS differences: GPS smoothing, satellite lock, or sensor calibration can make group-ride speed/distance data look better. If you use a power meter or heart-rate monitor, comparing those metrics is helpful.

Step 3 — how to check which factor(s) are responsible (practical tests)
- Compare objective data: review your Garmin logs for solo vs. group rides. Look at average speed, average power (if you have a power meter), normalized power, and average heart rate. If speed is higher but power/heart rate is similar or lower, drafting/route/wind are likely. If speed and power both increase, you probably simply ride harder in the group.
- Check cadence and interval patterns: steadier cadence and fewer accelerations on group rides suggest better pacing/drafting.
- Repeat a familiar route both solo and in the group under similar conditions to isolate the group effect.
- Check mechanics: measure tire pressure before solo and group rides, ensure chain/cassette are clean/lubed, confirm no brake rub.
- Look at environmental data: wind direction, temperature, and route elevation in ride logs.

Step 4 — recommendations you can act on now
- If you like the improvement, try to reproduce the aspects you can control: keep drivetrain clean and lubed, maintain optimal tire pressure, and adopt the same warm-up/fueling routine you use before group rides.
- Use your Garmin data to quantify differences (power vs. speed vs. heart rate). If you don’t have a power meter, heart rate and perceived exertion still help.
- Practice group-riding skills (drafting, rotating smoothly) so you can reliably benefit from pack dynamics.
- If you want to test mechanical gains vs. group effect, do a solo time trial on the same route and compare metrics.

Short answer: yes—very likely reasons include the new drivetrain (less friction), drafting and steadier pacing in a group (big aerodynamic gain), better routes/conditions, and higher motivation—use your Garmin metrics and a few controlled tests to pinpoint which factor is dominant.

   - If you frequently need centralized access (streaming, sharing large media, remote access), automated scheduled backups from multiple devices, or worry about single-drive failure on the external HDD, buying now is reasonable.

2. Security and reliability considerations
   - A NAS adds convenience but also requires maintenance (firmware/security updates, account hardening). If you’re ready to manage these, buying now is fine.
   - If your current backup is a single external drive, that’s a single point of failure. A NAS with RAID (and a separate offsite/cloud copy) would improve redundancy — a good reason not to delay if data loss would be costly.

3. Capacity and future growth
   - If your storage needs are small and stable, a 2-bay NAS is a cost-effective start.
   - If you expect growth, camera surveillance, lots of media, or want RAID 5 later, get a 4-bay for flexibility. If you’re undecided, waiting while you track growth for a month or two is fine.

4. Timing and price
   - NAS units and HDDs go on sale at predictable times (Prime Day, Back-to-School in late summer, Black Friday/Cyber Monday). If price sensitivity matters, waiting for one of these sales can save money.
   - HDD prices can fluctuate; if you spot a good deal on NAS-grade drives (WD Red, Seagate IronWolf), you could buy drives now and pick the NAS chassis later — but compatibility/return policies matter.

5. Practical recommendation (decision logic)
   - Buy now if:
     - You need automated, centralized backups or remote access today.
     - You’re worried about redundancy because your external drive is your only copy.
     - You want features like mobile-photo auto-backup, media streaming, or surveillance support immediately.
     - You’re prepared to handle basic NAS maintenance and security hardening.
   - Wait if:
     - Your existing external backup is up-to-date and you can tolerate the current workflow short-term.
     - You want to shop for the best price (next sale) or haven’t finalized how much capacity/raid you’ll need.
     - You’d like time to research models and read recent firmware/security reports.

- Configure security: enable HTTPS, change default ports, set strong passwords, enable 2FA, apply automatic updates, limit remote access or use vendor secure services (QuickConnect, myQNAPcloud) correctly.
- Implement 3-2-1 backup: keep at least one offsite or cloud copy of critical data.

Step 4 — concrete next steps (if you wait)

Based on that, here are targeted ways to give chocolate chip cookies “something extra,” with why and how to do each:

Flavor boosts
- Brown the butter: browning adds deep nutty/caramel notes that make cookies taste richer. Replace the same amount of butter with browned-then-cooled butter.  
- Use a darker / molasses sugar: swap some granulated or light brown sugar for muscovado or demerara (start with 2–3 tbsp, or replace up to 25–50% of the brown sugar) to add toffee/molasses depth.  
- Add espresso/instant coffee powder (1 tsp per batch): enhances and intensifies chocolate flavor without tasting like coffee.  
- Add vanilla + almond extract: 1 tsp vanilla + 1/4 tsp almond extract lifts flavor complexity.  
- Zest or spice accents (optional): a little orange zest, a pinch of cinnamon or malt powder can make the chocolate pop.

Texture & structure
- Chill the dough 24–48 hours: develops flavor and prevents over-spreading (better chew + deeper flavor).  
- Add an extra egg yolk (or use 1 whole egg + 1 yolk): for chewiness and richness.  
- Use a mix of flours: some bakers use a bit of bread flour (for chew) or a touch of almond flour for tenderness—don’t swap fully unless you want a big texture change.  
- Underbake slightly: pull when edges are set but centers still soft for a gooey interior.

Add-ins & finishing touches
- High‑quality chocolate chunks (mix chopped bars + chips): chunks melt into pockets; chips give structure.  
- Toasted nuts (walnuts, pecans, or sliced almonds): toast then chop and fold in for crunch and toasty flavor.  
- Toffee or caramel bits: adds chew and caramel notes that work with muscovado/turbinado.  
- Sprinkle flaky sea salt (a few flakes) right after baking: the contrast makes flavors sing.  
- Sprinkle a little turbinado or demerara sugar on top before baking for a crunchy, caramelized top.

A simple experiment to try (one-batch combo)
1. Brown 1 cup (2 sticks) butter until nutty; cool.  
2. Cream with 1 cup packed dark brown sugar (or 3/4 cup brown + 1/4 cup muscovado) + 1/2 cup granulated.  
3. Add 1 whole egg + 1 egg yolk, 1 tsp vanilla, 1/4 tsp almond extract, 1 tsp instant espresso powder.  
4. Fold in 2 cups all‑purpose flour, 1 tsp baking soda, 1/2 tsp salt.  
5. Stir in 10–12 oz chopped dark chocolate (mix chunks + chips) and 1/2 cup toasted chopped nuts (optional).  
6. Chill dough 24 hours. Scoop, sprinkle a pinch of turbinado sugar and a flake of sea salt on each ball, bake at 350°F until edges are set but centers still soft.

That combo hits caramel/toffee notes (muscovado + browned butter), intensified chocolate (espresso + good chocolate), crunch and contrast (toasted nuts + turbinado + flaky salt), and ideal texture (extra yolk + chill + slight underbake).

Step 2 — reason over that information and explain what each process does:
- Atmospheric distillation: the first primary refining step where heated crude is separated into boiling‑range fractions (gases, naphtha, kerosene, diesel/gasoil, and heavier residues) for further processing.
- Fluid catalytic cracking (FCC): breaks heavier gas‑oil/residual fractions into lighter, higher‑value products (gasoline, diesel range hydrocarbons and light olefins) using heat, hydrogen transfer and a catalyst.
- Alkylation: combines light olefins (from FCC) with isobutane over an acid catalyst to produce alkylate — a high‑octane, low‑sulfur gasoline blending component.
- Hydrotreating: treats various streams with hydrogen over catalysts to remove sulfur, nitrogen and other contaminants and to saturate unsaturated compounds so products meet fuel quality and emissions specifications.

Note: actual unit configuration and operating details can vary with feedstock and market needs, but those four are the primary processes listed earlier for the Lake Charles refinery.

  - Check neck profile (how it feels in your hand), fretboard radius, string action, and whether you can comfortably play chords and fingerstyle up and down the neck.
  - Look for fret buzz when you dig in, and check intonation by fretting notes at the 12th and higher frets.
- Hardware and build quality
  - Inspect tuners (smoothness, stability), bridge (intonation adjustments), nut, binding, finish, and neck joint. Wiggle the strings and neck to detect loose parts.
  - For used guitars: check for cracks, repaired headstock, replaced necks, or dodgy solder joints.
- Electronics
  - Test each pickup position and tone/volume pots for crackling. If the model has coil‑split/tap, flip it and compare single‑coil‑like tone vs humbucker tone — make sure the switching is clean and useful.
  - Listen for hum or noise in single‑coil modes; see if the split is usable live.
- Weight and balance
  - Les Pauls tend to be heavier — make sure the weight is comfortable and the guitar balances on a strap without neck dive.
- Sustain, resonance, and acoustic tone
  - Play unplugged and listen to the guitar’s acoustic resonance and sustain — this matters for fingerpicking and unplugged dynamics.
- Setup and practicalities
  - Ask the store about the guitar’s setup (string gauge, action, intonation). If you like it but want changes, ask for a professional setup quote.
  - Check warranty, return policy, and whether a case or gig bag is included.
  - If buying used, ask about history, serial number, and any modifications.
- Accessories and follow‑ups
  - Plan to buy or bring the strings gauge you prefer, a good strap, and a hardshell case if you travel.
  - Consider upgrades later (locking tuners, different pickups, a professional setup) rather than rejecting a great guitar for something that’s easily changed.
- Final practical checklist to bring to the store
  - Comfortable shoes/standing stamina, photo ID (if demo rooms require it), favorite pick(s) or a small pedalboard if testing effects, and a short list of specific things to play (open D riff, chords, lead lines).

Short summary recommendation
- At the store, prioritize feel and playability first (neck, balance), then tone and electronics (including coil‑split behavior), then build quality and setup. Try the exact styles you plan to play (open D, fingerpicking, heavy riffs) so your decision reflects real use. If you want both Les Paul warmth and Strat‑like clarity, give extra attention to Les Pauls with coil‑split/tap or try semi‑hollows and versatile pickup configs.

Step 2 — reasoned, practical advice to improve your slow cooker results
General slow-cooker technique (works for meat, veg, stews, chilis)
1. Brown first (when appropriate)
   - Sear meat and sauté onions/garlic briefly before adding to the slow cooker. Browning builds flavor (Maillard reaction) that otherwise won’t develop in the low, moist cooker.

2. Mind layering and liquid
   - Put firmer vegetables (carrots, potatoes) on the bottom near the heat; put meat on top.
   - Use less liquid than you think — the slow cooker traps steam. For stews, start with 1–1.5 cups of liquid for a 4–6 qt cooker and adjust. You can always thin at the end.

3. Low and slow is usually best
   - Use LOW for most recipes (6–8 hours) for tender meat and better texture. HIGH cooks faster but can dry proteins and over-soften vegetables.

4. Don’t lift the lid
   - Every lid lift adds ~20–30 minutes of cooking time and lets heat/steam escape. Only check near the end.

5. Vegetable timing
   - Root veg and squash: ok at start.
   - Quick-cooking veg (peas, greens, zucchini) — add in last 30–60 minutes to avoid mush.

6. Cut sizes matter
   - Uniform, slightly larger chunks for slow cooking so they hold shape. Small pieces can disintegrate.

7. Use the right cuts of meat
   - Tough, inexpensive cuts with connective tissue (chuck roast, pork shoulder, lamb shanks) become tender and flavorful. Lean cuts can dry out.

8. Finish for texture and flavor
   - Thicken sauce at the end with a cornstarch slurry (1 tbsp cornstarch + 1 tbsp cold water, stir into hot liquid) or reduce on the stovetop.
   - Add delicate herbs (basil, parsley) at the end; add hardy dried herbs early.
   - Brighten with acid (vinegar or lemon) at the end to lift flavors.

9. Season carefully
   - Salt early for meat and beans (but be cautious with reduced liquids). For some recipes, salting too early can firm beans/veg; taste and adjust at the end.

10. Prevent burning on bottom
   - Avoid high sugar sauces or jam-like glazes for long cooks on HIGH; add sticky sauces later or cook on LOW. Ensure there’s some liquid beneath sugary glazes.

Vegetarian/vegan slow-cooker specifics
1. Dried beans vs canned
   - If using dried beans: soak first and either pre-boil (safer to avoid slow-cooker toxin risk) or ensure long LOW cooking; some beans (kidney) should be boiled 10 mins before slow cooking.
   - Using canned beans: add in last 1–2 hours to avoid breakdown.

2. Texture for plant proteins
   - Tofu/tempeh: add in last 1–2 hours to avoid them falling apart (unless you want shredded texture).
   - Lentils: cook times vary — red lentils break down (good for dals), green/brown hold shape.

3. Creamy elements
   - Nut milks/coconut milk: add in last 30–60 minutes to avoid curdling; coconut cream holds up better.
   - For vegan creaminess, add blended beans/pureed veg at the end.

4. Layer flavors
   - Toast ground spices in a pan first, or bloom them in a small amount of oil to deepen spice flavor before adding.

Slow-cooker yogurt (dairy and cashew) — troubleshooting and tips
1. Use a thermometer for consistency
   - Heat milk to 180–185°F (82–85°C) to denature proteins and kill unwanted bacteria. Cool to 110–120°F (43–49°C) before adding starter. Thermometer use avoids inconsistent batches.

2. Starter and incubation
   - Use 2–3 tbsp of active plain yogurt (with live cultures) per half gallon milk, or a measured probiotic/vegan yogurt starter per product instructions.
   - Incubate 8–12 hours (longer = tangier/thicker). Keep temperature steady ~110°F during incubation—wrap the slow cooker in towels or use a yogurt function/insulated cooler if needed.

3. Cashew-based yogurt specifics
   - Soak cashews 4 hours or overnight (longer makes them softer and easier to blend).
   - Blend with water: start with ~1:1 cashews to water (by volume) and adjust: less water = thicker. Blend until completely smooth (2+ minutes in a high-speed blender).
   - Strain through a nut milk bag or fine sieve for ultra-smooth texture.
   - Use a vegan starter/probiotic strains designed for plant-based ferments. Plant-based “yogurt” cultures can behave differently — follow starter instructions.
   - Heat is still relevant: if using nut milk, warm to incubation temperature (not scorching) before adding starter.
   - If texture is runny: try adding a thickener (agar, tapioca starch, or gelatin alternative for non-vegan use) or refrigerate longer; making it “Greek-style” by straining helps.

4. Prevent failure
   - Avoid adding sweeteners or acidic fruit before incubation — they can inhibit cultures. Add those after yogurt sets.
   - If your yogurt doesn’t set: probable causes are insufficient heating/pasteurization, starter too old, incubation too cool/short, or killed cultures (milk too hot when adding starter).

Quick fixes for common slow-cooker problems
- Runny stew/sauce: remove some liquid and boil down on stove, or add cornstarch slurry.
- Dry meat: too high temp or overcooking — rehydrate with broth and cook short time till tender; next time use LOW and consider fattier cuts.
- Mushy veg: add delicate veg later.
- Bland flavor: brown ingredients first, add salt/acidity at end, and finish with fresh herbs.
- Burnt bottom: reduce heat setting and increase liquid; avoid sugary marinades early.

Small checklist before starting a slow-cooker recipe
- Do I need to brown/sauté first? (Yes for most meat/aromatic veg)
- Are my veg/meat cut to similar sizes?
- How much liquid? (Start modestly)
- Will I cook on LOW or HIGH? (Prefer LOW for tenderness)
